Mr. G. G. McGEER (Vancouver-Burrard) moved the second reading of Bill No. 27, respecting British Columbia Telephone Company.

Mr. Speaker, had it not been for the discussion of all these technicalities I would have been half way through my speech by this time. However, I take it I may now proceed.
While the bill deals with only one company doing business entirely within the province of British Columbia, it raises for consideration certain principles which are of vital importance to Canada at this time. Accordingly I feel justified in asking members of the house to give this bill the most careful consideration.
The principles involved are, first, under what circumstances should a company whose works have been declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, and which has been

British Columbia Telephone Company
incorporated by an act of this parliament, be given power to increase its capital at this time, and, second, should the powers of a public utility company, enjoying the monopoly of a public service, in this case the telephone service over most of British Columbia, be extended at this time.
The British Columbia Telephone Company was incorporated under the name "Western Canada Telephone Company" by a private act of this parliament in 1916, to be found as chapter 66 of the statutes of that year. The present bill seeks to amend the original act of 1916. As I have indicated already, the original act declared that the works authorized were works for the general advantage of Canada. Under that act power was given to the Western Canada Telephone Company to take over a company then operating a telephone service in British Columbia and known as the British Columbia Telephone Company Limited, and thereupon to use the name. This was done in 1919. At that time and for several years following the company was controlled by local people in British Columbia.
A few years ago, however, during the boom years, this control was acquired by the Associated Telephone and Telegraph Company of Kansas City and it is still held by that company. The control is through another subsidiary company known as the Anglo-Canadian Telephone Company, which holds all the common stock of the British Columbia Telephone Company, with the possible exception of a few qualifying shares for directors. The par value of the common stock is $4,500,000.
As I have said, the company is controlled in reality by the Associated Telephone and Telegraph Company. Also the parent company controls through Anglo-Canadian several smaller telephone companies in British Columbia-Chilliwack Telephones Limited, Kootenay Telephone Company, Limited, Northwest Telephone Company, and Mission Telephone Company Limited-all of them actually operated by the British Columbia Telephone Company, the company which is asking that this bill be passed. So that in essence the British Columbia Telephone Company has virtually a monopoly of the telephone business in British Columbia. I think there are two exceptions: The Okanagan Telephone Company of the Okanagan valley and the municipal telephone system in the city of Prince Rupert. The British Columbia Telephone Company is an efficient company, efficiently staffed and carrying on
business in an efficient way; it is doing a cash business and admittedly an exceedingly prosperous one.
Now the company comes to this house asking an amendment to its charter. First of all it asks under section 3 of the bill that power be given to the directors and shareholders to increase the capital stock from $10,000,000 up to a maximum amount of $20,000,000; in other words, power to double the capital stock. Section 3 also contains a subsection which provides that before the stock is actually issued or sold, approval must be obtained from the board of transport commissioners. But I submit to the house that the question whether or not power should be given to the company to increase its capital is one for this house to decide, that it is not a matter to be settled by the board of transport commissioners. That board has only to do with the details of when and how the new stock shall be issued. The bill also asks for certain extensions of the powers which the company already possesses.
I propose to deal first with the question of increasing the capital stock. By the act of 1916 the capital of the company was set at $5,000,000, with power given to the shareholders to increase that amount up to a maximum of S10,000,000. Throughout the years advantage has been taken of that provision until at the present time the company has issued stock to a value of $10,000,000,
SI,000,000 of which consists of 6 per cent cumulative preference shares, $4,500,000 of 6 per cent preferred shares and the remaining $4,500,000 of ordinary shares. In addition there have been bonds issued to a total of $12,500,000 bearing interest at 4J per cent. Now the company is asking for power to double its capital from $10,000,000 to $20,000,000.
I think that the house should consider the wisdom of granting or refusing this request from several different points of view, and in the first place from the point of view of Canada's war effort.
If power is given to make this increase it may mean the raising of $10,000,000 from the people of British Columbia or certainly from the people of Canada, in war time. I suggest to the members that such power should only be given under circumstances which are exceptional. The granting of such power now, in other words, should be the exception rather than the rule. I would remind the house of what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) said to us earlier in the week. It will be found at page 2343 of
British Columbia

Telephone Company
Hansard. In outlining the task which is faced by the Canadian people in raising the money that will be required the Minister of Finance said:
It will require also the careful limitation of our commercial and industrial investment to such plant and equipment as will aid in carrying on the war and as is necessary to the maintenance of essential services.
He then, announced that the government was going to control investment for the first time, and he said :
This policy of controlling investment will have the important effect of providing a larger market for government bonds.
Surely this bill brings up this very question. Are we to follow the wish of the Minister of Finance or are we not? The raising of this additional capital by the company will be in direct conflict with the attempt of the Canadian government to raise money, and the terms will be far more favourable than any terms the Canadian government can offer. This company has been paying steadily six per cent to the preferred shareholders, and it has been paying eight per cent on the common stock issue of $4,500,000, with the exception of one or two years during the depression. Just imagine the effect on the sale of war savings certificates in the province of British Columbia if it should be announced that this company has been given power to increase its capital and eventually it puts new shares on the market! It may mean that there will be up to $10,000,000 less to be put into Canada's war effort. Besides that, it would be an example for other companies to follow in other parts of the nation. It does seem to me that this whole subject might well be left for consideration after the war.
So much from the point of view of the effect upon Canada's war effort. Now let us look at the company's request from the point of view of the necessity for issuing new shares and acquiring fresh capital. I can find no necessity ^hown for such an increase at this time. It is true that there has been an increase in the number of telephones installed by the company. I have here the annual statement for the calendar year 1940 and on the back there is a chart of the installations of telephones over the years. It was not until 1937, a little over three years ago, that the company once again had as many telephones in use as in the year 1930-in other words, got back to its position of eleven years ago.
Mention was made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, when he explained this bill on first reading, of the fact that some municipal authorities on the coast have agreed not to oppose this bill. But at the time they gave the bill consideration they did not have

before them this annual statement for the year 1940. It did not come out until the end of February. Nor did they consider the bill from the point of view of its effect upon the war effort, because they were under no obligation to do so.
In 1940, as this statement shows, 5,914 telephones were installed by the company, many of them for the fighting forces, for the various army, navy and air force headquarters in British Columbia. In other words, they are temporary installations; and while they are temporary, you can be sure they will be paid for; the telephone company will suffer no loss on these war installations. In 1941, I am told by the president of the company, the company expects to make around 5,000 installations, a decrease of 900 from the year 1940.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer), speaking the other day, said, as reported at page 2297 of Hansard:
The cost of the installation of such services-
Referring to new services at the rate of 5,000 to 6,000 a year.
-runs from $1,000,000 to $1,250,000 a year.
That works out at $200 per installation, which, I suggest to the house, is entirely too high, in fact is absurd. I believe that the real
reason why heavy capital expenditures have been made is set out in newspaper reports of March 1, 1941. In the Vancouver Province, the issue of that day, we find this statement:
f sheet discloses that nearly vAOOO.OOO of capital expenditure was made, chiefly in Vancouver in connection with the conversion from manual to dial equipment.
Nothing at all to do with the installation of new phones, but the change-over to the new dial system.
Additional outlay on this account will be made in the first part of 1941, after which it is planned to defer capital expenditure as much as possible until after the war.
I believe that the installation of this automatic equipment is what has called for the bulk of the capital expenditure, and most of this expansion has already taken place. At least as the newspaper report says, it is to be deferred, the change-over is to be stopped now until after the war. But, even with these capital expenditures which have already been made, the accounts for the calendar year 1940 show a net profit of $659,000 out of an operating revenue of $6,050,000. For the sake of clarity I am giving the figures in round thousands.

I will explain that as I go along. Depreciation of $998,000 is written off for last year-which is very heavy for one year, particularly in view of the fact that over the last twenty-four years the total depreciation, including what is written off for last year, is only $8,522,000. Taxes amounted to $627,000, being $209,000 more than in 1939. In other words, despite increased taxes and despite heavy depreciation, there was a net profit of $659,000. The balance carried over from 1939 was $537,000, and after paying dividends for last year of 6 per cent on preferred and 8 per cent on common stock, the balance on December 31, 1940, stood at $506,000. We find from the balance sheet that there was cash in the bank amounting to $461,000 at the end of last year and in going through the assets we find other assets which are fairly liquid; for example, bonds of the Northwest Telephone Company, amounting to $255,000, and bonds of the city of Vancouver -which I am sure the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard will agree are liquid, since they were issued when he was mayor of our city- amounting to $53,000.
Surely some of this money could be used for expansion for war purposes. Surely the dividends on the common stock could be reduced. If the rate for this year were cut from 8 per cent to 3 per cent, $225,000 would thereby become available to apply on the cost of the telephone extensions which are necessary this year. Surely the parent company, the Associated Telephone and Telegraph company, could do a little sacrificing. They would get their money in the end- at any rate after the war.
Surely there could be a cessation of further heavy commitments by this company, for example, in changing over telephones from manual to automatic. It should defer such capital expenditures until after the war. In so doing the company would suffer little hardship, and could apply at that time, if it were so desired, for power to increase the capital.
I come to my final reason why power should not be given at this time, under war conditions, to increase the capital stock of this company. Many readjustments in our civilization will result from the present war. Make no mistake about it, there will be great readjustments in Canada, and almost certainly in regard to public services such as telephone service. The Canadian people may wish to have their governments take over such public services; in fact in some provinces the governments already operate the telephone service. Increases now of the capital of public utility companies will make such readjustments more difficult, and may even cause grave trouble.
So much for the request for power to increase the capital stock. Before I conclude I should like to say a few words with regard to granting extended powers at this time to a public utility company which enjoys a virtual monopoly. If hon. members will turn to section 2 of the bill they will see it has to do with the issue of preference shares. I have no objection to a company being given power to issue preference shares in the future under new tennis, but, as I read this section, it gives the company power not only to do that but to change the status of the present preferred shares. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, when he spoke the other day, said that as the law stands at the present time the preferred shares which have been issued cannot be redeemed.
They have always had a good market value; the price has been above par practically all the time, and to all intents and purposes apparently they are perpetual shares. Sales have been made by one holder to another throughout the years; people have bought these shares with all the rights which now pertain to them, yet under paragraph (c) in section 2 of the bill we find that the company is given certain powers over those shares that have already been issued, including power to redeem them under certain conditions. In other words this is a provision which is a distinct benefit to the company and a distinct detriment to the holders of the preferred shares. It is not fair to ask this house to pass legislation of that type, in war time or at any other time.
Section 5 of the bill gives the company power to buy shares of a company carrying on business of a similar nature. When this company received its original charter it was given power to buy only the physical assets of another telephone company; it could not buy the shares of that company. Now in this section the company is given power to go out and buy shares; and, as I read the section, even to buy shares in a company operating a radio station, for example, thus going far beyond the original powers. The restriction was there before; why should it be removed by this bill?
Another section which should be carefully checked by members of the house is section 6, which gives the company power to carry on not only telephone and radiotelephone services-which latter is a very necessary service on our coast and which has been carried on very well by this company-but also services for the transmission of sound, pictures, writing, or signals by means of any device, apparatus, system or method of whatsoever nature, whether now in existence or which may be discovered or developed in the future. One

printed explanation of the bill eipressly mentions television. This company is to have power to go into the business of television, and I think that goes too far. Before these wide powers are granted, particularly at this time, the whole question should be most carefully reviewed by this house. Television probably should be handled by the government of Canada; I do not know by what body, but presumably by the broadcasting corporation. Certainly before we give any private company power to handle television we should know exactly what we are doing and why we are doing it.
That concludes my remarks with regard to this bill. I have been greatly concerned about it because I want to be fair, not only to the people who sent me here, the other people of my city of Vancouver and the people of British Columbia, but also to the telephone company. I am convinced that this bill should not be passed during the war, that the position should not be changed at the present time; that if passed it will probably interfere with our war effort and give the company powers which it should not have, or which, in any event, should be given only in peace time and then after the most careful consideration.

The bill now before the house, Mr. Speaker, is second from the bottom in the list of private bills numbering some forty-eight appearing on the order paper for to-day. The British Columbia Telephone company is a very dominant influence in British Columbia, but. I did not know that it had sufficient influence to reach out three thousand miles and have its bill taken from almost the bottom of the list and placed at the top, and have it debated at a time when, under our rules, private bills should not be called at all.
The sponsor of the bill did not follow the usual custom-I admit that it is only a custom-of giving an explanation of the bill on the motion for second reading. Therefore we must depend on the few remarks he made when he introduced the bill; but I have no doubt he will take advantage of his privilege of closing the debate to answer all the objections that may be advanced up to that time. I would point out to hon. members of this house however, that under our rules the sponsor of the bill closes the debate when he speaks at that time, and there can be no further debate on the question, so that it will be impossible for any of those who oppose the bill to reply to any statements he may make, however willing or able they may be to do so.
I have been requested by some of my constituents to oppose this bill. I do so quite 
willingly, despite the fact that before this debate is concluded I am sure once more the accusation will be made which is so lightly thrown across the floor of the house these days, that we are holding up our war effort. But the bill has been brought in under these circumstances, and I think it is our duty at least to comment upon it. As I understand it, if this bill is given second reading it will go to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I hope on that committee there will be someone with sufficient determination to gain for us a great deal of information that we do not now possess and that we should have before we are asked to pass the bill.
I endorse, so far as my lay mind could follow them, the legal objections raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), and I wish to quote as well a resolution which has come into my hands. This resolution was passed by the Vancouver Community Council, the nature of which I will explain in a moment. The resolution states:
The Vancouver Community Council, an organization representing all the community associations 9f Vancouver, B.C., do hereby protest, along with the citizens' committee, to any increase in capitalization of the B.C. Telephone Company Limited during wartime, mainly because we are of the belief that this company will seriously deprive the government of enormous sums of taxes by such increased capitalization.
We are also of the belief that the B.C. Telephone Company Limited are taking advantage, at this time, of the public having their concerted attention centred on the all-important problem of winning the war, therefore expecting less opposition than at normal times.
The company are showing in their returns that they are paying six and eight per cent dividends which naturally sets up an opposition to the war savings stamps campaign, when the government can only pay less than three per cent.
We have examined their annual report and financial statement and are convinced that the application now before the board of railway commissioners of Canada is not of sufficient merit to warrant an increase in capital at the present time. No valid or substantiated reason has been advanced by the company as a basis for enlarging the capita] structure; that if there are reasons, the public should be notified as to the reasons-particularly in view of the tremendous increase petitioned for. The public, being vitally interested in the proposed increase, should know why the capital will be underwritten; by whom; when the cash capital realized will be expended, how so expended, and where expended.
We believe that any increase in capital would necessarily mean an increase in telephone rates, and the people of Vancouver cannot afford any increase and at the same time keep up with the demands of the government for funds to carry on the war.
I will now explain the nature of the Vancouver Community Council. It seems

British Columbia Telephone Company
that it is a council composed of delegates from a number of community associations, and they give the names of sixteen well known suburbs or parts of Vancouver. I think I am justified in saying that it is a large and respectable body; large, as indicated by all these sixteen associations, and respectable because of the men associated with them. The honorary president is Mayor J. W. Cornett of Vancouver. The mayor of Vancouver is not a man picked up in the gutter. Among the names of other vice-presidents I read that of R. Rowe Holland, B.A., a well known lawyer and Dr. G. M. Weir, a cabinet minister in British Columbia, and last but by no means least Mr. G. G. McGeer, K.C., M.P.
I believe he is the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, and I am prepared to accept implicitly 'his endorsation of this association from the fact that he is an honorary vice-president.
The objections, as they appear to me, are as follows: First, the amount is too large; certainly just now, as it undoubtedly will affect the campaign for the government loan soon coming on. I myself have $2,000 I was going to put into that government loan at three per cent or whatever it may be, but being of Scottish origin I may be strongly-tempted to put it into the six per cent bonds of this company. And I am sure there will be a great many other people subject to the same temptation; for a great deal of the $10,000,000 will be raised from the people of Vancouver or British Columbia. No sufficient reason has been given yet that I have heard why such a large sum is needed now. The balance Sheet does not indicate that it is more than at most partly necessary. That this is apparent to the bill's sponsors will be seen by the remark of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard on introducing the bill, as reported on page 2298 of Hansard.
This is a statement made by a talented lawyer who knows the value of words and what language is intended to convey.
I should like to make it clear that this amendment does not authorize an increase in the company's capital of another $10,000,000; it merely authorizes the company to make application from time to time to the board of transport commissioners as new capital issues are required to sustain the progress of its service.
Well, let us see what the bill does say. Section 3 reads:
6. (1) The capital stock of the company may be increased from time to time by such amounts as the directors consider requisite for the due carrying out of the objects of the company,
Is not that clear enough? And there is a limitation that it shall not exceed $20,000,000. Which statement is correct? I submit the one in the bill is the one that will be given effect to, perhaps in the law courts, in years to come.
Let the hon. member read subsection 2 if he wants to be fair.

I shall come to that. The sponsor said that it "merely" authorizes the company to go to the transport board. The word "merely" gives the whole show away. This is what subsection 2 says-and it is not the section, it is only a subsection of it, separate and distinct.
(2) The company shall not have power to make any issue, sale or other disposition of its capital stock or any part thereof, without first obtaining the approval! of the Board of Transport Commissoiners for Canada of the amount, terms or conditions of such issue, sale or other disposition of such capital stock.
What are they to give approval of? Of this bill? Not at all; we are giving approval of the bill. When this bill passes this house and the senate it is final; no one else can dispute or reject it, unless it is unconstitutional, and that is not even suggested. So that when we pass it it is final and irrevocable law, not subject to the approval of anyone else, man, god or angel. The details of the bond issue are subject to the approval of the board of transport commissioners; they can say, Oh, we think that at the present moment $8,000,000 or $6,000,000 is perhaps enough; or, we do not like the terms. But they have no control whatever over the authority to issue $10,000,000. And I venture to predict that the second paragraph of the application to the board will read something like this: "And whereas the Parliament of Canada has authorized this company to increase its capitalization by $10,000,000." I am no lawyer, but that is common sense, which sometimes is better than law.
The board cannot reverse our legislation and say to this company: You cannot issue $10,000,000. They might defer it, or say go slow, or change the rate of interest, but they cannot upset our legislation. And that is perfectly well known to these people who drew up this bill. So we can dismiss that argument, which at best means that they say: Give us power to increase to $10,000,000, but in case it sounds too rank we will sugar-coat the pill by saying: "We will take the amount in sections." And eventually they will get the whole $10,000,000. And they cannot be denied by anyone short of this parliament, and now is the time to do it. It may be alleged that they do not want the $10,000,000 now and do not intend to issue any of the bonds. Then why ask for the power? They have got along for twenty-four years with $10,000,000; if they do not need more now -why ask for more? If they are asking for it then you can take anyone's word that if they get the power they will use it.

So that the question is, is it wise to allow them now, when money is so badly needed for war purposes, to issue $10,000,000 of new capital at six per cent, possibly to compete with the government issue at three per cent?
Much has been made of the statement of the council of the city of Vancouver and the council of municipalities. We are told that these councils have not opposed the bill. It appears from the statement which I have now heard for the first time-we have no evidence for it-that they had not even read the balance sheet. Yet they give their approval. It now appears that it was not an approval or authorization but merely a decision not to oppose. Rather weak support, isn't it? We would like our constituents to give us more definite support than that. The Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals is not opposing this bill, but that does not say it approves the bill. If everyone is held to approve who has not said anything against it, that does not look very strong. I should like to see a copy of the resolution passed by the council of the city of Vancouver approving of this bill. I do not think it can be produced. And the same as to the council of municipalities. Perhaps the opposition of the council was softened by the assurance that, they could always oppose it before the board of transport commissioners. Yes, but they would soon get tired of going there; it costs money, and it would happen every few months. Did hon. members ever hear of Hitler s method ? Hitler is supposed never to do anything by ohance. He does not grab the whole hog at first; he grabs only a bit of it. You do not feel like fighting for that bit. Then by and by he wants more of it.

He starts on the hind
quarters.

But if he had asked for the whole hog in the beginning, you would object. They will take it all, I believe; I do not say they will do it now, but eventually they will get the whole ^ $10,000,000. But that will not prevent the city council and the council of municipalities from coming along in a year or two and howling their heads off if we allow this to go through. They will say they were misled, that they did not understand, and that it was our business to see that they were protected.
The hon, member sponsoring the bill has said that there are some other minor changes to be made. I turn to them now, because I am not so sure that these minor changes do not contain the nigger in the woodpile. Perhaps they are even more important than the actual capitalization provision. On introducing the bill the sponsor said th's:
There is an amendment-

And these are among the minor amendments-
-providing for the redemption of the preferred shares. The fact is that the preferred shares issued already by the company were issued in the terms of a contract which is redeemable. Technically-
"Technically"-
-the powers which the company enjoys under its present charter do not permit them to carry out the terms of that contract.
Hence, of course, it is to be amended giving them power to do so. Either it is yes or it is no. If the preference shares were issued long ago with power to redeem them, then this section is unnecessary. If they were not issued in terms by which they can be redeemed, then I say this section is unjust and unfair. This is an attempt to deprive preferred shareholders of privileges they possess. It deprives them of their rights. Because the shares were issued non-redeemable more money was obtained, and a better price was obtained when the shares were sold. No doubt more people were induced to invest, perhaps they invested more willingly and more money than they would otherwise have done. Now they are paying six per cent. The very fact that they are paying six per cent, and the perhaps more apparent fact that they were not redeemable- and we are told they were not-put the price up until the present market price is about 114. And they are going to be redeemed perhaps next month or next year at 100. Is that a square deal to the man who bought with the knowledge that they were not redeemable?
Had the company gone broke, the owners of the common stock would not have come forward, reimbursed the preferred shareholders and said, "You have had a raw deal." They would have said, "You have taken your risk and lost your money; there is no use whining about it." There used to be a day when investors who put money into an investment got an even break. If it turned out badly they lost all their money, and if it turned out well they made money. Nowadays investors are people who have been induced by prospectuses to put money into something. If it goes bad-well, it is just too bad; if it turns out to be a good thing, they are frozen out later on. Either they are redeemed out or, in the case of mining companies, there is another method which appears to be very effective. Who is going to reap the benefits from this deal of redeeming preferred stockholders? It will be the common stockholders, of course. And who are those W'ho hold the common shares? They are all held in the United States by people alien to us. The intention is to redeem these people who have

British Columbia Telephone Company
now a successful and profitable investment- indeed, so much so that they can get six per cent. So that these preferred stockholders are to be frozen out, and the benefit will fall into the maw or into the hands of the common stockholders-people who are not even resident in our country or our province.
Had the results been the other way round, had it lost money, would the common stockholders have taken it up? I do not think they would. The sponsor says that technically- "technically"-they cannot be redeemed. Now the purpose is to bring about a condition so that they can be redeemed. May I point out that the dial system is just being introduced to a large portion of the city of Vancouver. Most telephone companies, upon introducing the dial system, anticipate making money from that installation.

Yes, by laying off
employees.

That is the reason they do
it. Yes, the money is made by laying off the employees. They have no soul at all. They do not care when they have to lay off employees. They do it for one purpose and one only, namely, to make money. And the dial system having been introduced only a few months ago, they will certainly make more money. They are making eight per cent now on their common stock. There would be no harm done if they kept it at eight per cent, and allowed this surplus profit to go toward the capital they say they need so much.
Inevitably the increased capital will be used to ask for increased rates. They will say, "Now we have to pay an interest of eight per cent on $20,000,000." They will go to the board of transport commissioners and ask for that increase of rates; and no doubt when they urge that they ought to be allowed to make three per cent on $20,000,000 they will get permission. The larger capitalization is probably intended, in part, for that reason. The rates are now high enough.
I have no ill will against this company or any of its officials. It is a good company, and well managed. I believe it is managed almost too well for the common good. I have had transactions with it as an ordinary business man, and also as a member of parliament connected with government transactions, and I realize perfectly that the small business man had no look-in at all when it came to dealing with the British Columbia Telephone company in a matter of business. I would not take time to go into the painful details now, but it is sufficient to say that I have speedily discovered who paid the piper in that case.
So I believe it can be said that the company is shrewdly managed. I hold a few shares in the company, and I recognize with gratitude the regularity with which interest has been paid over a term of years. I am not afraid that the dividends will be reduced in the company -and, as I am a shareholder, I suppose I can say "our company." Our company will not lose by it, even if they are stopped from spoiling the market for $10,000,000 of government 3 per cent loan, or from robbing the shareholders by a forced redemption. Robbing is the word to use when you are taking away some one's rights, or a portion of them, by compulsion.
There are other objections to the bill which have been dealt with by the hon. member for Vancouver South. However I hope the committee will look into this matter, and I hope they will amend this bill so that if the company require a reasonable amount of capitalization it may be granted to them, but only a reasonable amount and without the other evils I have suggested.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about this bill which has already been analysed by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). Before I left Vancouver in the early part of February I was informed by the general manager, I believe it was, of the British Columbia Telephone company, that it was their intention to have a bill introduced amending the British Columbia Telephone Company Act. I met him and he explained the various sections of the bill to me. I told him I would keep an open mind in the matter.
I then notified the mayor of the city of Vancouver that a bill to amend the telephone company act was going to be introduced, and drew his attention to what I considered the important sections of the amending bill. As I suspected, the matter had already been drawn to the attention of the city council by the telephone company. I have before me a copy of a letter addressed to the city clerk of Vancouver by the corporation counsel. The letter is dated February 20, 1941, and reads:
Fred Howlett, Esq.,
City Clerk,
City Hall.
Re: B.C. Telephone Company and proposed amendment to its charter authorizing increased capital.
Dear Sir:
When this matter last came before the harbours, utilities and airport committee it recommended that the Fraser Valley reeves' association be asked to submit the reasons why

it was opposing the telephone company's application and it further recommended that the company be asked to undertake that any application to the board of transport commissioners for the issue of further stock should be upon notice to the city.
I understand that you have had no reply to the letter to the Fraser Valley reeves' association. On the question of notice to the city, after some negotiations with the general manager he finally agreed that the company should give such notice.
As a result I now have a letter from the president of the company, a copy of which is attached hereto.

I believe I have in my file, although I am not definitely certain, the covering letter from the city clerk, which accompanied this letter and which stated that an approving resolution had been passed by the city council of Vancouver. I did not concern myself further with the matter. Some little time ago, however, I received a letter from the Vancouver communities council, of which the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer), the sponsor of this bill, is one of the vice-presidents. The resolution passed by that body was read by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. It strenuously opposed the passing of the amending bill. It seems to me that the hon. member for Vancouver South has given sufficient proof that the interests of no one will be- injured by allowing this bill to stand over for the present time.
The company made application for a similar amendment in 1933. I believe the matter was allowed to stand over until 1934, and the bill was finally withdrawn. If the company found it could get along from 1934 to 1941 without this additional capital, it seems to me strange that an application should be made for increased capital at a time when the country stands so much in need of money for other purposes. Considering its strong liquid financial position, I am convinced that the interests of the British Columbia Telephone company will not suffer if this bill is withdrawn or its passage refused at the present time.
There are two procedures which we can follow. The house can decline to give the bill second reading, or it can agree to the

second reading and refer the bill to the proper committee where its supporters and those opposed may submit evidence to substantiate their claims. The other day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) announced in the budget a proposal which will make it more difficult for the ordinary citizen to provide himself with certain essentials of life. I think that gives parliament sufficient reason for refusing at this time to give its consent to increasing the capital stock of this company.
The budget proposal to which I made reference will discourage the building of homes in Canada, despite the fact that there is an urgent need for better housing. I believe the need is more urgent for housing and for improved social conditions than it is for this, in the main, luxury service, although, of course, it has an important commercial side. I think we can very well refuse to give second reading to this bill and allow the company to bring it forward at a more opportune time.

Would the sponsor of the bill be good enough to lay before the house the terms of the resolution under which the present preferred shares of this company were issued? There seems to be some question whether these shares are or are not redeemable. The explanatory note opposite section 2 of the bill which deals with the redemption of preference or preferred shares seems to include a paradoxical statement. It reads:
The purpose of this subsection is to enable the company to redeem preference shares issued as redeemable shares.

I have copies of the two preference share forms, the cumulative and the other. In both cases the provision for redemption appears on the share certificate. In one instance the certificate reads:
The company shall have the right to redeem

I was
referring to the resolution upon which the shares were issued.
Mr. MeGEER:	The resolution is incorporated in the share certificate.

The house will realize that we are debating the motion for the second reading. If the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) speaks now, he will close the debate.
Mr. KARL K. HOMUTH (Waterloo South): Mr. Speaker, we have been asked to take unprecedented action in putting this bill through in the way in which it is being put through. If the procedure is unprecedented, then I think hon. members should have a clear understanding of what the provisions of the bill mean. I realize that it may be difficult for

British Columbia Telephone Company
an hon. .member from another province to deal with something which appears to be a purely provincial matter and rather innocuous in form, but after listening to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) and the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill), one begins to realize just how far-reaching are the provisions of this bill. During this war-time session several bills have been introduced which could well have been left in abeyance. There is still on the order paper one bill providing for the giving away of some park land in Saskatchewan. A whole evening sitting of the house was taken up in discussing that bill, but we got nowhere with it and I do not think we shall get anywhere with it this session.
Here is another bill which, at first glance, does not appear to be serious, but when one delves into it he begins to realize that this large corporation is trying to extend its tentacles and gain control over things in British Columbia over which it has no control at the present time. Furthermore it is not exactly a Canadian concern. We are being asked to give this organization an opportunity to expand its capital structure, but as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has so well said, if we grant this privilege, this organization will go to the board of transport commissioners and, as has happened in this country before, will say to them: Here is our capital set-up on which we are entitled to earn at least such and such a dividend, and to do that we must increase our rates.
The explanation given to us was that the company was extending its service. The chart aecompanjdng the financial statement for 1940 shows how the service has extended, and I do not see how any company that has made the progress this one has, and with the earnings it has, can need to enlarge its capital. Just read the balance sheet of the company; see the reserves for depreciation and the depreciation written off every year; see the amount they provide for repairs and maintenance.
Again, just as the Bell Telephone company and other companies have done, this company is going to modernize its service. But all these modernizations of service mean laying off help. Public utilities never modernize their service unless it puts them in a position to make tremendous savings in power, staff and other matters that more than compensate them for the cost of modernizing. Modernizing its service is not going to cost this company anything because in the long run it will make tremendous savings. Throughout Ontario and other parts of Canada telephone companies have modernized
their service, and as a result thousands and thousands of employees have been laid off. The same sort of thing happens when an industrial corporation installs new machinery. It means that it is able to reduce labour costs and increase production.
Surely at a time like this, when there are other matters of much greater importance to Canada and to this parliament, we should not be asked to pass this bill increasing the capitalization of this company, particularly when, according to the company's own balance sheet, it is not necessary at all.
There is, further, this important consideration, that so long as we continue to make it possible for great monopolistic institutions such as this to issue new stock at six and eight per cent, we shall not be able to ask the people of this country to buy three per cent war bonds. If my industry or any industry in which any other member of this house is interested wishes to buy new machinery and extend its plant or do other things that may be necessary to the war effort we are making, we have not the right to do it, nor can we have a private bill introduced into the house in order to have it done. We have to go before the board that has been set up by the government, and this board tells us whether or not we may make the extension. Every private industry engaged in the manufacture of munitions or war materials is compelled to go before this board and get its approval before it can spend one cent on capital account. Yet here is this monopolistic telephone company, controlling the telephone business throughout British Columbia, in a position to come here with a private bill, which on the face of it looks as innocent almost as its sponsor, to increase its capitalization. I think this house should take a stand against this bill and refuse even to give it second reading.
I do not think the house should be asked to take other than the general course in dealing with bills of this kind. I do not know what the procedure in the House of Commons is with regard to such bills, but I know that in the legislature of Ontario a private bill must first go before the law officers of the crown. If the bill is contrary to government policy or to the best interests of a municipality or of the province, the government itself takes a stand and says: "This bill must not be proceeded with because it is against the interests of the municipality or contrary to the general law of the province and against its best interests, and we ask the sponsor to withdraw it because we think such legislation should not go through this house."

British Columbia Telephone Company
The law officers of the crown might well give all private bills of this kind careful consideration, and if it is found they are contrary to the best interests of the country or any section of the country, the government should take a stand and say that the legislation should not be allowed to pass through the house.
This is a serious matter, Mr. Speaker, and I think the members of the house ought not to acquiesce either in this application or in the manner in which it is presented.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) has mentioned that this bill is far-reaching. It reaches farther, I think, than any member of the house realizes because, if hon. gentlemen will look at section 6, starting at line thirty-four, they will find that it provides that this company:
. . . may operate wireless telephone and radio telephone services and services for the transmission of sound, pictures, writing, or signals by means of any device, apparatus, system or method of whatsoever nature, whether now in existence or which may he discovered or developed in the future.
If this bill should pass this house, it would mean that parliament was giving away the right to operate machines that might be developed in the future. What would have happened if radio stations had been given the right to operate like this before our broadcasting system was set up? We cannot tell what machines may be developed in the next few years. That clause should be thrown out; in fact, I think it is sufficient reason for throwing the whole bill out. We cannot tell what the future holds in the way of developments, and to grant this company these powers would be dangerous because, with the $20,000,000 behind it, it would have unlimited influence throughout the country and would be able to do almost anything under the sun. I agree with the hon. member for Waterloo South that we should refuse to give this bill a second reading.

The Fraser Valley reeves' association has been mentioned. I happen to be their representative, or I was last year when they asked me to oppose the bill. I took the matter up with the association and asked on what grounds they were opposing it. They withdrew their objections after certain amendments had been made. I am very much interested in these amendments which have been submitted to the reeves.
When I was home at the Easter recess, to find how much poorer the farmers in my district were getting, I had the objection thrown at me, as representing a farmers' 
riding, that we could not get a bill before this house to effect the reduction in freight rates which we should have had forty years ago, and which the present sponsor of this bill fought so hard at that time to get for us. I say, we could not get that reduction, yet this magnificent United States company can come in by a back-door-I believe we in this house should describe it as that "other place". Apparently all that that "other place" is doing this session is to pass a bill for a telephone company and handle divorce proceedings. I do not happen to know anything about these stocks and shares. As a farmer I have never had enough money to buy a share. I bought a few war savings stamps. But how I am going to sell war bonds I do not know. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) asks me to go home in June and endeavour to organize my riding to buy government bonds which must be sold to return three per cent, while other companies are going to be competing with me, selling bonds at six per cent.
The other objection I have to the bill is that, having been a municipal official, and knowing what happened to the British Columbia Electric company and the British Columbia Telephone company, I do not know who can guarantee that there will not be an increase in rates? I hope that the sponsor of this bill will use his influence with the British Columbia Telephone company to have conditions adjusted in my municipality, where, with some 5,500 people, we have three telephone exchanges-three long distance offices.^ Certainly we have a right to an adjustment in view of those conditions, exactly as we have the right to fight any increases, if we decide to do so, by appearing before the board of transport commissioners. But how could any municipality afford to send any of these famous Vancouver lawyers to Ottawa to fight? I know the lawyers would like to come. They have had plenty of fun fighting on behalf of the British Columbia farmers. But we cannot afford to send them. I believe the company should give us a guarantee that, at least for a period of years, there will not be an increase.
I may inform the sponsor of this bill that, although I had intended to vote for it, I am going to oppose it, and on one ground only, that I think the government of which I happen to be a supporter should reject it unless the company agrees to withdraw what neither this nor any other government has the right to legislate away-that which is now in existence or which may be discovered in the future. I certainly will not vote for any bill so long as it contains a clause of that kind.
