speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
There has been a good deal of misconception with regard to this bill; and, putting it fairly and not very strongly, I must say that from a legal point of view there has been some misstatement.
Evidently this company was a consolidation of a number of separate and existing companies away back in 1916. They received from parliament a charter which will be found in chapter 66 of statutes 6-7 George V, 1916. Although the company is one operating wholly within the territorial jurisdiction of British Columbia, it was evidently desired to form a dominion company by invoking the provisions of the British North America Act, because, under section 2 of the statute to incorporate the Western Canada Telephone company, afterwards changed to the "British Columbia" company, the works authorized were declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, which, of course, gives jurisdiction to this parliament.
Evidently the company went on and expanded, and it is now said that the authorized capital stock of $10,000,000 has been fully issued, subscribed and paid up. If I apprehend correctly, there are three distinct classes of shares-two kinds of preference shares, and the common or ordinary shares.
It is a matter of regret that the sponsor of the bill did not make an extended preliminary statement in moving the motion now before the house, because then we would have had from him a statement as to the exact position of the company with reference to the issue of its share capital. I attempted to get that information from the hon. gentleman, when Mr. Speaker intervened to state that, if he spoke at all, it would be by way of closing the debate; and we have not received the information.
What does the company ask for? One of the things it asks for is to be found in section 3 of the bill, which repeals section 6 of the original act dealing with the authorized capital stock of the company. Subsection 1 is purely enabling legislation; let there be no mistake about that. Parliament is asked to grant an increase of franchise authorizing the company, if it complies with certain considerations, to increase its capital stock from $10 million to S20 million; it provides the method by which the shareholders themselves may take the first ordinary steps with regard to that matter, and it puts a limitation of $20,000,000 on the total capital stock of the company to be issued.
If the company is expanding, of course there must be capital expenditure. One way of financing a public utility is by the issuing of
shares-not bonds, as some hon. gentlemen here have suggested. The company is not asking parliament to give any authority with respect to a bond issue. Under its charter it can issue bonds, by the authority of its shareholders, without coming to parliament. That, I believe, must be clear; at least, I would be very much astonished if it were not the situation. I have not seen the balance sheet, but I have no doubt it will show that there is an issue of bonds, which of course are the first charge on a company's assets. Let us be clear on that point.
A telephone company is a public utility; it cannot stand still. There have been in the last quarter of a century more developments, I suppose, made in scientific lines with respect to this great public utility than any other public utility that I know of, with the result that nearly evely community of any size or consequence has an automatic telephone system. What does that mean? It means that plant in which money was invested in days gone by has become obsolescent and, in many instances, is worth little more than scrap. It must be replaced, and it is for the purpose, in part, of replacing it that, under standard systems of accounting, telephone companies and public utilities of this kind are allowed, by the control bodies which have been set up in nearly every jurisdiction, such as public utilities commissions and, in the case of the dominion, by the board of transport commissioners, to set aside substantial sums, varying according to the category of the equipment.
The reserve that is set up-I do not know what it is in the case of this company, but it is characterized as a huge sum-is intended to take care not only of that but of all the unforeseen things that may happen to a public utility of this kind. Go down to the maritime provinces and go through a winter storm there. One storm may cost as much as $150,000. I have seen one storm cost the New' Brunswick Telephone company $100,000. That is paid out of the reserve which is set up for just such contingencies. There is nothing improper about that; it has to be done. You cannot call upon the shareholders to make good dead losses of that sort; you cannot ask the subscribers to increase their rate. These reserves are set up because business judgment, experience and foresight visualize these things, and there is nothing per se wrong about a public utility of this kind having set up, under the authority of law and under the judicial bodies that govern that sort of thing, substantial reserves for depreciation, obsolescence and so on. Let us have that clear.
2512	COMMONS
British Columbia Telephone Company
Therefore I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that any argument based upon the theory that over a period of twenty-four or twenty-five years this company has been able to set aside a large reserve for depreciation is not in itself a condemnation of the company. Let us be judicial about this. Because of that reserve the company is able to take care of certain things in times of stress; it is able to go on and adopt new and improved methods of telephonic communication, in part out of reserves and in part out of new capital. The capital expenditure of a company of this kind is never at a standstill. It is like any other big industry; every year some capital expenditures must be made in order to keep up with the demands on the company itself. If this company is growing at the rate of five thousand telephone outlets a year, I suggest that it is making great progress and is serving an increasing public.
In passing, may I suggest that the rates charged by a telephone company are based not on what the traffic will bear but on the service it gives to a community, subject to the imprimatur of a judicial body which fixes those rates. Primarily the telephone rates of any community are based on the number of outlets that a telephone company serves. In a community of ten thousand people with, we will say, three thousand telephones, one standard rate is fixed. In a community of fifty thousand people, with perhaps ten thousand telephones, a higher rate is paid, because that exchange serves a much wider purpose, and a subscriber is able to reach that many more people. Therefore let us have it clear that capitalization per se has nothing whatever to do with rates. That is a fair statement; and I do not think any hon. gentleman who has investigated the position will disagree with it. Capitalization has nothing to do with rates; and the fact that this company is asking for an authorization to issue stock under certain circumstances- not for the issue of stock-does not carry with it as a necessary consequence that the rates will be increased, as my hon. friend seems to fear. I think that is a fair statement to make, and I am prepared to substantiate it. But the company must go ahead; it must have new capital on which it can draw to take care of these capital expenditures, and that is one of the primary things for which this company is asking.
What are the safeguards with respect to this company? They are exactly the same as are set up in relation to the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. I remember, as I am sure my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will remember, the battles in this house and this city years ago 
over the applications made by the Bell Telephone company to increase its capital stock. This company, like the Bell Telephone company, is under federal jurisdiction; and before it can do anything in the way of issuing stock, aside from the ordinary corporate proceeding of getting the authority of its shareholders, it must make public application to the board of transport commissioners; it must give public notice to all concerned, and it must prove its case. I think that is a fair statement.
That is right.

At least it must make out a strong prima facie case before it can get any authority at all. In addition to that, the board of transport commissioners have power not only to say that the company shall or you shall not issue new stock, but also to say at what rate that stock shall be issued by the company. I remember the great battle that followed the last application of the Bell Telephone company, with regard to the very question of the figure at which the stock should issue. If my recollection is right, the order was made that the new issue of Bell Telephone shares be fixed at $125 a share. Therefore it is not altogether true to say that people are getting eight per cent on their investment in connection with the Bell Telephone. I fancy that the rate of return on Bell Telephone common shares is very much less than eight per cent on the average, because in many instances the proprietors have put more than par into the new extensions.
All right. In addition to that, the board of transport commissioners has power to impose other conditions and obligations upon this company. For instance, in subsection 2 of section 3 of itihe bill there is this provision:
The company shall not have power to make any issue, sale or other disposition of its capital stock or any part thereof, without first obtaining the approval of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada of the amount-
They have to show absolutely, dollar for dollar, what they require to issue.
-terms or conditions of such issue, sale or other disposition of such capital stock.
I suggest to the house that under those circumstances, where we set up a judicial body to deal with these measures, aside altogether from the question of whether or not it is expedient to do this in war time, with which I am not going to deal, there are due safeguards with respect to the issue of new capital stock.
So far, perhaps I may be said to have been arguing my hon. friend's case, but I am afraid I must say to him that I really cannot go very

British Columbia Telephone Company
much further for him and still maintain a judicial attitude. There is something wrong; there is a coloured gentleman somewhere in this bill, with respect to this question of redeemable or irredeemable preferred stock, about which we have not been told. If the stock is redeemable in the terms of the issuing resolution as authorized by the original legislation and the corporate proceedings of that company, then I suggest that this portion of the bill which deals with the redemption of the presently outstanding shares is unnecessary. I do not know, for I have not been able to see the resolution.
That is the nigger.

My hon. friend may be right; I am afraid of it. But what I think the company is attempting is to put itself for future issues of preferred stock in the comfortable position that the English Companies' Act gives them. If I were acting for the company I would certainly strive to get that. If this company were applying for the right to issue preferred shares at this time de novo, probably parliament would give them the rights of issue as laid down by the English Companies' Act of 1929. I see no great objection to it.
What are preferred shares? Preferred shares are a form of capital introduced into a company to finance that company's capital operations. I never knew of a case where a company sold preferred shares to take care of operating deficits. You just could not sell them if a company were in that position. Companies sometimes issue preferred shares rather than bonds, they are a form of loan to companies; loans, we will say, upon which it is not obligatory to pay dividends in certain instances, or the dividends may be cumulative or non-cumulative. But preference shares are a form of aid and assistance to a company which it, when it prospers, may pay off and redeem. When it does, it should have two or three options. If it redeems and cancels, then its share capital should be reduced accordingly; or it may have the right to refund by the same method only on different terms.
I do not know what the position is with respect to the preferred shares of this company; it has not been divulged to this house, and before this bill goes through, it should be abundantly clear that there is no breach of contract with the present holders of the preferred shares. If the shares are irredeemable, the company should not be given the right by legislation of this parliament to take away the contractual rights of these preferred shareholders, many of whom, I suggest the majority, were not the original subscribers for
these shares. They are bought on the public market on the theory that it is a perpetual stock upon which the company can, when it is earned-I assume that condition-pay six per cent interest. That must be made clear to me before I can support this bill. If the sponsor of the bill can show me that there is no breach of contract with these preferred shareholders, that the company is only exercising the original legal rights granted when their charter was issued-

If they have the right
under the charter, why have it in this bill?

That is the question I have been asking myself. Observe this statement in the explanatory notes to sections 1 and 2 of the bill:
2. Subsection three of section five is new.
I have indicated why it is new; they want to take advantage of the existing provisions of the English Companies' Act; I think that is clear.
The purpose of this subsection is to enable the company to redeem preference shares issued as redeemable shares.
If that is the purpose, they do not have to come to parliament; at least I make that as a prima facie statement. There is some reason which has not been told for them to ask that authority, because if they have it under the original charter they do not need to come here for it.
Then, turning to the succeeding paragraphs, we find a number of them, all of which are quite proper if the authority is required and if the company is to be given a new power to issue new preference shares. For instance, if these shares are cancelled, then under the provisions of the Companies' Act, 1934, the parliament of Canada has provided that such shares shall be cancelled; the Secretary of State may issue a certificate confirming the reduction of capital, on such terms and conditions as he thinks fit, and the company does not have to come back for supplementary letters patent. That is merely a matter of procedure.
Then paragraph (b):
(b) no preference or preferred shares shall be redeemed unless they are fully paid and no premium shall be payable on the redemption of such shares except out of profits which would otherwise have been available for dividend.
That, of course, is a proper provision, that any premium on these shares must be paid out of profits, not out of capital; otherwise the capital of the company would be impaired.
The other paragraphs are not so important. Paragraph (d) leaves the right of re-issue unimpaired, and I think that is probably what they want.
2514	COMMONS
British Columbia Telephone Company
Note the words "heretofore or hereafter'' in the .preceding paragraph.
Look at section 6 of the 1916 act.

Yes, I am coming to that. I wish to deal for a moment with section 4 of the bill. I see no objection to this section; it provides that, notwithstanding the provisions of our Companies' Act which limits the number of the directors I think ito nine, they may have up to eleven. That is merely a matter of internal management.
Section 5 of this bill is an extension of a principle that was certainly not contemplated at the time this act was originally passed; and may I say that the provisions with respect to investments in the original act were exceedingly conservative, and to my view proper provisions to .put into a public utility company act. In the original charter -this company could only invest moneys of the company, including surplus and sinking fund money not immediately required for the purpose of the company, in trustee securities. That is absolutely sound. That .principle is reincorporated in section 5, but has a tremendous extension. They may do almost anything, so long as it is related to the electrical business. They may, for example, reach out and grab any of the broadcasting stations in British Columbia. I do not know that that is contemplated, but it is possible.
Mr. GREEN; The directors do it, not the shareholders.
Well, the directors must be acting for the company.
Not necessarily.

Oh, I would think so. Section 16 of the original act defines the powers of the company.

I have made reference to paragraph (i) under section 5, which appears on the opposite page of the bill. This is the section which deals with the investments. Under the new proposed section the company-not the directors, but of course the directors are the moving force in the company with respect to these matters-are to "subscribe for, take or otherwise acquire and hold shares and securities of any other company which furnishes facilities for electrical transmission." They may own power stations, power plants, power transmission lines and so on. Then it continues, "of communications or intelligence by sound or signal," and so on.
In other words this section gives the company power to invest the surplus money of the company in any kind of scheme in furtherance of the business of the company. If I may be frank with the hon. member who sponsors the bill, I do not like that feature.
Under section 6 very far-reaching powers are sought by the company. In the discussion on first reading reference was made to radiotelephone, and there was the statement that it was now in operation. If it is in operation, then it is operating under the authority of the charter. That must be so, without question. If they have the power now, then they do not require it through this bill. I believe an important question is raised in section 6, because although the section is made subject to the provisions of The Radio Act of 1938, and subject to the provisions of other statutes in Canada relating to radio and radio broadcasting, and to the regulations made thereunder- of course the company must come under those regulations-the section goes on to ask for authority to operate "wireless telephones and radiotelephone services, and services for the transmission of sound, pictures, writing, or signals by means of any device, apparatus," and so on.
Parliament may want to give the company this right, but I do not think it is part of the business of a telephone company. I should assume that they already have facilities for radiotelephone service; if they have not, they ought to, because telephone companies are the only people who can give that service. But if they are placed in a new field of electrical transmission business, which may be projected in the immediate future, they will claim a prescriptive or exclusive right. They should not have that power.
That is about all I have to say in the matter.
I believe we ought to pass the part of the bill which involves the principle of providing enabling authority to increase the capital.

British Columbia Telephone Company
Except to the Minister of Finance.

My hon.
friend says, "except to the Minister of Finance." That raises an important question. Are we to stop the growth of corporations of this kind by reason of the necessity of war? Each one of us will have to answer that question for himself. I do not think we can stop the progress of a public utility of this kind because of a war. As a matter of fact I would suggest that the increased facilities of a company of this kind might be very beneficial in time of war.

It might bring in United
States money, too.

Yes, it
might bring new capital. My hon. friends assume that the new shares will be sold in British Columbia. I would suggest to the people of British Columbia that if this company is as well managed as is indicated in the balance sheet it would be a good thing for them to get in on it. In fact I would not mind having some of these shares myself, if they are as good as that.

Buy war savings
certificates.

Of course, that is a factor to be considered. But that means setting up the principle that there shall be no progress for the duration of the war in connection with the activities of a public utility corporation of this kind. It may be necessary; it may be that we shall have to come to that point. Perhaps it is a factor which might well be left to the board of transport commissioners-unless this parliament is going to establish now the principle that there shall be no expansion in any kind of industry. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth), we have gone a long way by order in council under the War Measures Act toward controlling and curtailing expansion of capital expenditures in certain lines of industry. Whether or not we should do it in connection with a corporation of this kind, I cannot say. My personal view is that the company should have the enabling legislation asked for in connection with the increase of capital stock, but that every other portion of the bill should be scrutinized with the greatest care.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a private
bill which, having been passed by the senate, has been introduced in this house. Having had the approval of that august chamber we
may assume that it has been thoroughly considered, because those hon. gentlemen usually complain that they have not enough work to do.
They mean public, not private bills.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Enough work in general. However, this is a private bill. The discussion on the second reading is merely as to the principle. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) has clearly stated, and it is set out in an explanatory note, that the principle of the bill is that of obtaining an increase in capital from $10,000,000 to $20,000,000. It is said that that amount is necessary to provide facilities adequate for the needs of the service in British Columbia. It is indicated that the company should have new property, and that it is particularly necessary to direct the development of the lower mainland and Vancouver island.
The rules governing second reading of a private bill are about the same as those for a public bill, but with this very great difference, that the approval is given conditionally. In this connection I shall read two annotations from Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms concerning the second reading of private bills. Paragraph 865 is as follows:
The second reading of a private bill corresponds with the same stage in other bills, and in agreeing to it the house affirms the general principle, or expediency, of the measure. There is, however, a distinction between the second reading of a public and of a private bill, which should not be overlooked. A public bill being founded on reason of state policy, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, accepts and affirms those reasons; but the expediency of a private bill, being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill, conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee. Where, irrespective of such facts, the principle is objectionable, the house will not consent to the second reading; but otherwise, the expediency of the measure is usually left for the consideration of the committee. This is the first occasion on which the bill is before the house otherwise than pro forma or in connection with the standing orders; and if the bill be opposed, upon its principle, it is the proper time for attempting its defeat.
And then, paragraph 867:
The house does not profess to decide upon the second reading as to the truth or otherwise of the allegations of fact upon which a proposed bill is based, and in conceding a second reading to a private bill the house is regarded as merely giving its sanction to its general principle on the hypothesis that the committee to which it is afterwards referred finds those allegations proved. It is usual, therefore, to allow the second reading, except when the bill enunciates some principle which the house is not prepared to affirm.

2516	COMMONS
British Columbia Telephone Company
The only principle which should be considered on this motion for second reading is whether the company should be granted the increase in capital for which it is applying.

This bill is a general
amendment to an act which has been passed and there are other principles involved than the mere increasing of capital.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That was another private bill. All the sections of the bill may be struck out in committee, and that is where it should be considered. Are we in position to say that the improvement of the position of this company as far as properties and other developments are concerned will not be for the good of the province of British Columbia? I believe the promoters of the bill should have an opportunity of presenting themselves before a committee, and it should be for the committee to decide whether these rights and privileges should be granted to this corporation. I do not think we should take the stand of refusing this corporation the right to come and explain this matter before the railway committee. The hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) and another hon. gentleman have said that this bill looks innocent, perhaps too innocent. I cannot see what harm will be done by giving second reading to a bill which looks so innocent. If it is found to be bad after it comes before the committee, that will be time enough then to defeat its passage.

Mr. Speaker, I came into the house this afternoon with an open mind so far as this particular bill was concerned, although I may have some bias in favour of public ownership. After hearing the various arguments, particularly the one advanced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) just now, I find myself in some disagreement with him. The minister quoted from Beauchesne to the effect that if the allegations upon which representations are made in support of the second reading of this bill are found in the committee to be unfounded, then the house need not subsequently accept the bill.
We are considering this bill under somewhat special circumstances. This week we had introduced the largest budget of expenditures ever introduced in this house. The tremendous amount of money which will have to be raised, either by loans or by other means, will require every dollar that is available in the country for investment. Therefore we ought to consider to what extent a bill of this kind will impinge upon public necessity and public policy. We must consider to what extent a public utility of this

sort should be permitted to go before the public to obtain funds which might otherwise be available for the necessities of the nation. This feature should receive the consideration of the house before the bill goes to committee.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) has said that we should consider whether we are ready to adopt the principle that a public utility should not be permitted to expand its capital in war time. I listened carefully to the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) and I think he showed quite clearly that this company has paid what is to-day a high return upon its capital, a rate of eight per cent. He suggested, I think with reason, that if the company would reduce this rate of dividend or profit to three per cent, the difference might be utilized for capital expansion and the extension of facilities. It has been shown also that the company has an investment in city of Vancouver and other bonds, and that these are sufficiently liquid to be realized upon. I realize that that will interfere somewhat with the argument I advanced first.
Before this bill goes to the committee I think we should decide whether the circumstances of this company and the necessities of the nation are such as to justify the granting of this call for additional capital at this time. I have no hesitation in saying that my own reaction would be in the negative. I would oppose the bill on the grounds I have indicated, as well as on other grounds.
The hon. member for Vancouver South and the leader of the opposition referred to the wide powers in connection with television and so on being granted by this bill. They go far beyond anything that now -exists, because any further developments or discoveries in these fields will accrue to the advantage of the company if these powers are granted. These are things which might properly come before a committee and which need not be the subject of much debate at the moment.
But I do submit that the other consideration which I have advanced, the necessity of this country raising vast sums of money by taxation and the realization that there is a tremendous gap of over a billion dollars which is not covered by taxation or in any other way, ought to be considered. So far as I am concerned I feel that until the necessities of the nation have been provided for we have no right to give even tacit approval to a bill which will enable a company, which has other resources and which may not need the money, to go out and obtain from the public funds which we ourselves will need badly in the near future.

Labour Condilions-Government Policy

Mr. Speaker, I fail to see why there should be such haste in attempting to put through this legislation. It might almost be called indecent haste. This bill is No. 47 on the order paper and we are being asked to consider it ahead of forty-six other items of business which precede it on the order paper. The discusssion of this bill has held up the vote of S35,000,000 which we have been considering and the other general estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
As hon. members have properly said, this company, which has a monopoly of the telephone business in British Columbia, is asking for the right to offer most attractive shares to the public, shares which will bear interest rates of from six to eight per cent. These shares will be sold in opposition to government loans and war savings certificates which bear interest rates of only three per cent. The people are being urged to buy these war loans and war savings certificates and I am sure that no complaint would be raised if they did not receive even the low rate of three per cent. They will be lucky if they get their money back.
The present powers of this monopolistic company are now sought to be greatly enlarged so that they will become not merely a telephone company but may go into television, money lending, the moving picture business, and what-not if this bill goes through. There is one thing they certainly should do, and I say this knowing the city of Vancouver, and having lived there for a good many years and taken part in its private and public life. The city of Vancouver is beautifully situated, but it will never be a beautiful city while its streets are hampered and disfigured by a forest of hideous telephone poles and sagging, unsightly wires which a company with the wealth of this one could very well conceal underground in the modern way. If they came to this house and said they wanted money for that purpose, I would be more in favour of supporting their application. But in the meantime I -can see no reason why the time of the house should be taken up in discussing this legislation further.
On motion of Mr. Mayhew the debate was adjourned.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of what took place this week in connection with the National Steel Car plant, when the government, under the authority of the War Measures Act, took over the plant on the plea that there had been a stoppage of production of war materials and supplies, and in view of the situation at present existing in relation to the Peck Rolling Mills in Montreal, will the Minister of Labour and/or the Minister of Munitions at an early day state the policy of the government in relation to the labour problem now confronting the country, and will the government afford an early opportunity for a discussion of labour policy and the whole labour situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY AND OPPORTUNITY FOR DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) is engaged in other business at present. In view of the broad questions which the leader of the opposition has asked, of Which he was kind enough to give me notice, I do not think I would be in a position at the present time to afford him a reply as to the time when the general problem of labour policy might be most appropriately discussed in the house.
He has mentioned the names of the Hamilton branch of the National Steel Car Corporation and of the Peck Rolling Mills of Montreal. There is an essential difference, Mr. Speaker, between the two companies. The National Steel Car Corporation at Hamilton had contracts from the government of Canada for the manufacture of munitions and
Labour Conditions-Shipping

war supplies. The Peck Rolling Mills of Montreal had none and have none from the government.
I might suggest, without going into a detailed discussion at the present time, whihh I think the leader of the opposition will agree would not be appropriate, that the dispute involving the National Steel Car Corporation was referred to a 'board, and that board brought in an interim report.
Advertisements have appeared in the papers addressed by the president of the company to its shareholders, and unquestionably that is his undoubted privilege. But I did not think that this was a matter in which any statement could appropriately be made in connection with the facts as stated in the advertisement because the matter is still under consideration by the board. The board's present report is purely an interim one. Certain statements are made in the advertisement, but I do not think this is the appropriate time to discuss them, except to say that the board was appointed for the purpose of determining the facts. My information is that certain statements made in the advertisement do not coincide with the evidence given before the board at its interim sittings. But it would be unfair for me to go into a statement of the allegations made, in view of the fact that the matter is before the board. To determine the facts and report upon them is the function of the board.
The government of Canada, however, has another function, namely, to keep the stream of war materials flowing without interruption, to keep the logs and the underbrush clear from that stream; and in taking the action which it did the government gave recognition to that extremely important function at the present time. May I suggest, however, Mr. Speaker, without going into too much detail at the moment, that whether that stream is clogged by employers or by employees, in either event the government of Canada realizes the importance of keeping the war materials flowing in its uninterrupted course.

maintopic: BACON BOARD IN CREASED PRICES FOR EXPORTS TO GREAT BRITAIN

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: BACON BOARD IN CREASED PRICES FOR EXPORTS TO GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext:
In
view of the statement in this morning's press that higher prices are to be paid by the bacon board for bacon shipped to the United Kingdom, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture.
According to the press statement the bacon board will pay an extra $1 per hundred pounds to packers for bacon exported to Britain, making the price for grade A No. 1 Wiltshire sides $17.10 per hundred pounds, and the new price goes into effect on "all products put into cure for export from hogs purchased on and after May 2." The report goes on to say that the additional payment by the bacon board will increase prices in the domestic market and thus cut down consumption and have a stabilizing effect on prices within Canada. Hon. J. G. Taggart, Saskatchewan agriculture minister and bacon board chairman, said he could not say whether the additional $1 per 100 pounds would be carried by the United Kingdom or Canada. He said announcement in this respect would be made later by federal authorities.
The United States government announced it proposed to hold live hog prices near the $9 mark to encourage production.
I would therefore like to ask the Minister of Agriculture: (1) What steps are being taken to assure that this increased prjce will reach the Canadian producers? (2) Has the Canadian government any plans to hold live hog
prices similar to the United States government plan? (3) Will the extra $1 per hundred pounds be carried by the United Kingdom or Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: BACON BOARD IN CREASED PRICES FOR EXPORTS TO GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was kind enough to give me a copy of the questions which he proposed to ask. I would reply as follows:
Owing to higher prices in the United States hog market, and increased demand in the Canadian domestic market for pork products, the bacon board has been unable to meet the request of the British Ministry of Food to forward larger weekly shipments of bacon to the United Kingdom. To obtain larger supplies for export the bacon board has increased the price of bacon by $1 per one hundred pounds, following an agreement with the British Ministry of Food that the price of bacon for shipment to the United Kingdom would be increased 5 shillings per 112 pounds at seaboard for the balance of the contract, with the understanding that any further advances which may be necessary to secure the required supplies will be met by the Canadian government, and that should lower prices obtain as a result of changes in the United States hog prices, the price of bacon to the United Kingdom will be adjusted accordingly.
It will be recalled, Mr. Speaker, that on reporting the agreement with Great Britain to the house, I indicated to the house that there was an undertaking that if the price of hogs went up in the United States to a point which endangered the shipment of bacon to Great Britain, the price would be reconsidered. The price has been reconsidered, and an offer in accordance with the terms I have just recited has been made to the bacon board by the British government and has been accepted by this government.
The hon. member's first question is: What steps are being taken to assure that the increased price will reach Canadian producers? The same steps as have been taken in the agreement up to date. That is, the matter is under consideration at all times by the bacon board; they are getting in contact with the different organizations which are purchasing from farmers here and there across Canada, and seeing that the prices do bear a proper relationship to the price being paid.

maintopic: BACON BOARD IN CREASED PRICES FOR EXPORTS TO GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext: What about the stocks in storage in the hands of the packers?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: BACON BOARD IN CREASED PRICES FOR EXPORTS TO GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext:
The stocks in storage that have to do with this trade have been put in storage on order of the bacon board.
Bacon Board

maintopic: BACON BOARD IN CREASED PRICES FOR EXPORTS TO GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext: So that they have control?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: BACON BOARD IN CREASED PRICES FOR EXPORTS TO GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: BACON BOARD IN CREASED PRICES FOR EXPORTS TO GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext: It is effective only after May 2, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: BACON BOARD IN CREASED PRICES FOR EXPORTS TO GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext: The order was made effective yesterday, May 1.

maintopic: BACON BOARD IN CREASED PRICES FOR EXPORTS TO GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext: But that is not to apply to bacon already processed, is it?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: BACON BOARD IN CREASED PRICES FOR EXPORTS TO GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext:
No, not to bacon already processed.
The next question is whether the Canadian government has any plans to hold live hog prices similar to the United States government plan. WTell, as I understand the United States government plan, it is operated under the surplus purchasing 'board which has been functioning for some time in the United States, purchasing surplus food supplies and distributing them, I think on the issue of stamps, to persons who are on relief or otherwise unable to purchase, and in other ways to people who would not use as large quantities of these commodities. My understanding is that that same board is empowered at present to purchase certain food products, including hogs, on the different markets in the United States, and some of them may be distributed under the lease-lend act to the British market as well as to the United States market. That is the only control that I know of, and it is exercised only by purchasing off the market from time to time. We have had in effect exactly the same thing ever since the British agreement came into effect in 1939. That is, we have been purchasing all the surplus hogs off the Canadian market and shipping them to Great Britain under that agreement, which resulted, in the year 1940, in hogs standing at a level of an average of about three cents higher than the market price. The United States during that period were buying certain surpluses, but not sufficient to keep their price up; there was too large a production of hogs.
The next question is whether the extra $1 per one hundred pounds will be carried by the United Kingdom or Canada. That is explained in the answer which I have already given. Under certain circumstances it will be carried by Britain and in other circumstances it will be carried by Canada, as indicated in the statement I just made.

maintopic: BACON BOARD IN CREASED PRICES FOR EXPORTS TO GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext: It will be the same as a bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: BACON BOARD IN CREASED PRICES FOR EXPORTS TO GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext:
No, it will not be the same as a bonus. The price now paid by the British is five shillings higher than it was. Under the original agreement it was 80 shillings per 112 pounds; it is now 85 shillings
[Mr. Gnrdiner.?
per 100 pounds, which results in there being available about one cent a pound more, or $1 a hundred pounds. If the price should advance beyond 85 shillings on the United States market, the Canadian government undertakes to be responsible for that increased amount, and if it drops on the United States market, we have taken on ourselves the obligation of reducing the price to Great Britain by the amount of that drop below 85 shillings.

maintopic: BACON BOARD IN CREASED PRICES FOR EXPORTS TO GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext: I did not send a copy of this question to the minister, but perhaps I may ask whether we are to understand that if the price goes either up or down in the United States, our hog prices will be governed accordingly?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: BACON BOARD IN CREASED PRICES FOR EXPORTS TO GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext: I would assume so, Mr. Speaker. That has been the effect so far. We should then have to make the choice whether we were going to purchase supplies on this market at a price which would compete with the United States price and send them to Great Britain. If we did that, under this agreement with Great Britain the Canadian government would have to bear the expense.

Where a farmer has followed the practice of varying his acreage from year to year, it is our desire to encourage him to start at the top of his 1940 wheat acreage and reduce it as far as possible.
Provision has been made in another subsection of the regulations to take care of cases where the variation has been one-third or more, which would indicate that the farmer was doing something during 1940 which it had not been his custom to do. In the cases where the variation has not been greater than one-third, no matter what percentage of his cultivated acreage he may have had in wheat, it is not our intention to reduce the point at which he starts his reduction of wheat acreage. In other words, there is not a maximum set for the acreage of all farmers; it was only some particular cases. There is always the possibility and the probability that where a man's records do show ninety per cent last year and seventy per cent the year before, such acreage is associated in some way with land which has been newly broken up, and if the man actually did have the land in wheat last year it would not be fair to ask him to start at some other level.
On the other hand, it is not a reasonable thing for a man to sow all his land to wheat two years in succession. The only case I can conceive of where that would be reasonable would be in cases where a man had land broken up in 1938 and all seeded to wheat in 1939, back-set in 1939 after the crop was taken off and then seeded to wheat again in 1940. That is quite legitimate; that can happen.

The information is as follows:
Officials of the wheat board are being continually asked by farmers to answer the question -"How much wheat can I market in 1941-42?" It is an extremely difficult question to answer in advance, that is, until we know the size and distribution of the 1941 harvest. Any figure given now may prove to he quite incorrect and the best answer is probably to be found by going into considerable detail.
The dominion government has authorized the Canadian wheat board to restrict marketings of w'heat in Canada to a total of 230,000,000 bushels. This means that wheat producers in the western provinces will be able to market about 223,000,000 bushels of wheat between August 1, 1941 and July 31, 1942.
In carrying out this restriction of wheat deliveries during 1941-42, the dominion government has authorized the Canadian wheat board to limit deliveries of W'heat from producers (to the Canadian wheat board, the open market or any other purchaser) in the w'estern provinces to wheat produced on 65 per cent of their 1940 acreages. This applies to individual producers.
For example: If a wheat producer had 100 acres of w'heat in 1940, his w'heat marketing quota will be calculated on 65 acres in 1941-42;
If a wheat producer had 200 acres of wheat in 1940, his wheat marketing quota will be calculated on 130 acres in 1941-42;
If a w'heat producer had 300 acres of wheat in 1940, his w'heat marketing quota will be calculated on 195 acres in 1941-42.
As a start toward calculation^ his marketing quota, each farmer can take 65 per cent of his sworn acreage on the 1940 permit book or if he has already surrendered his permit book, he can get the figure from the board. Certain exceptions to the 65 per cent rule have already been made for farmers with excessively large or small 1940 wheat acreage in proportion to the size of their farms.
Having the wheat acreage upon which the 1941-42 wheat deliveries will be based, the producer will then want some idea as to the number of bushels he can deliver. And here the difficulty arises because there is no way of forecasting the size of the crop in advance nor the distribution of the crop at the various yields, high and low.
If w'heat acreage in 1941 is reduced to 65 per cent of 1940 acreages, only a relatively high yield per acre could cause surplus wheat production to materially exceed the 223,000,000 bushels which can be marketed during 1941-42.
If, however, there is not a full reduction in wheat acreage in 1941, and if a high yield per acre is harvested, it will be necessary for the Canadian w'heat board to impose restrictions on the quantity of w'heat which can be marketed from 65 per cent of 1940 acreages. The extent of these restrictions w'ill depend upon 1941 sowm acreage and the average yield per acre harvested in 1941.

Supply-Agriculture-Wheat Acreages
If it is necessary to restrict marketings from 65 per cent of 1940 acreages, then the amount of wheat which must be held on farms over and above the 223,000,000 bushels which can be marketed will be distributed among all farmers on an equitable basis, excepting only those having very low yields per acre. Such farmers will probably be able to market all the wheat grown, except their seed and feed.
Except under abnormally high yelds per acre in 1941, the board believes that the major restriction in limiting wheat deliveries to
223.000.	000 bushels in the western provinces will result from the 65 per cent acreage basis for 1941-42 delivery quotas. This means that farmers can look forward to delivering from 65 per cent of their wheat acreage, either all their 1941 production from this acreage if the 1941 yield is light or moderate, or the average yield per acre in their district, less their proportionate share of the wheat which must be held on farms if the 1941 yield is heavy.
Wheat producers are justified in assuming that if there is a full reduction in acreage in 1941, and if an average yield per acre is harvested in 1941, they will be able to deliver in 1941-42 the greater part of the average yield per acre harvested in their district from 65 per cent of their 1940 wheat acreages. At the present time, it is impossible to say what the per-acre quota will be on 65 per cent of 1940 wheat acreage, other than the above general statement.
We repeat that any one figure for wheat marketings per acre, given at this time, is a pure guess. However, we can make this statement: If the full acreage reduction of 35 per cent, or more, is realized and if the general yield per acre is about average, then the producers will be able to deliver in 1941-42 a high proportion of the production on 65 per cent of their 1940 acreage.
The question as to what we would do if we had a crop the size of this year, is considerably more complicated, as we still feel that it would be impossible under a condition such as this to operate on a flat quota per acre basis. We feel that we would have to have a graduated scale based on the average yield for each district. This would still give an advantage to the low yield man as it would be unlikely that a farmer with a crop of ten bushels or less would be called upon to hold back more than a bushel or a bushel and a half per acre at the most. The heaviest burden would fall on the man with the high yield, but at the same time his rights would be recognized to some extent, which we feel is the fairest way it could be handled.
However, as mentioned above, this cannot be finally settled until probably August at the earliest, and with the probability of a material acreage reduction it would seem that the chances of the crop being much above
350.000.	000 are not very good.
In connection with implementing this policy, the Canadian wheat board announces the following decisions of special interest to wheat producers throughout the western provinces.
1.	Producers who seeded no wheat in 1940.
There are some farmers in the western provinces who, for one reason or another, did not seed any wheat in 1940 and therefore did not have 1940-41 delivery permits. Such farmers who desire to seed and deliver wheat in 1941 should make application to the board at their earliest convenience. Their cases will be considered, and if warranted, delivery quotas will be arranged for 1941-42. All applications must be made to the hoard prior to May 31, 1941. In his application the producer should give the legal description of his land and state his total farm acreage, the number of acres in coarse grains, summer-fallow, etc., and the delivery point to be used in 1941-42.
2.	Producers who seeded an abnormally small
proportion of their land to wheat in 1940.
There are some individual farmers who in 1940 had, for one reason or another, abnormally small wheat acreages. In these cases the Canadian wheat board will, on application of the producers concerned, review their wheat acreage position before establishing their delivery quotas for 1941-42. In making such an application each wheat producer must show that his 1940 acreage was substantially lower than his wheat acreage in 1939, and lower than the acreage which he usually sows to wheat. These applications for a review of 1940 wheat acreages must be in the hands of the board as soon as possible, and no applications will be received after May 31, 1941. Upon receipt of application, forms will be mailed to the producer upon which his case can be stated.
3.	Producers who seeded an abnormally large
proportion of their land to wheat in 1940.
An examination of 1940 permits issued by the Canadian wheat board shows that in most districts throughout the west, a few producers had abnormally high wheat acreages in 1940, compared with their total farm acreage. In so far as these wheat acreages are substantially higher than usual for the farms concerned, the Canadian wheat board will, in establishing 1941-42 delivery quotas for these farmers, make such adjustments in their 1940 acreage figures as will bring them into line with their usual practice and into line with their district as a whole. This means that wheat producers who unduly expanded their wheat acreage in 1940 will have their 1941-42 delivery quotas established on the basis of wheat produced on 65 per cent of their usual wheat acreage, and in arriving at the adjustment which will be made in these exceptionally large wheat acreages in 1940, the board will consider the practice of the other farms in the district, as reported to us.
As an example, a relatively few farmers in the western provinces had over 90 per cent of their total farm area in wheat in 1940. It would he obviously unfair to the great majority of wheat producers to extend delivery quotas to these few farmers based upon wheat produced on 65 per cent of 1940 acreages. In these cases delivery quotas in 1941-42 will be based upon 65 per cent of their usual wheat acreage and the average percentage of the farm land sown to wheat in 1940 in the district concerned.
The Canadian wheat board has adopted the foregoing policies in respect to the basis of 1941-42 wheat quotas in the interests of a fair distribution of quotas among wheat producers in 194142. The object is to adjust some of the wide variations from usual practice that occurred in 1940 wheat seeding.
